text:
The history of computation and mathematics draws on foundational work from figures like Al-Khwarizmi, Gottlob Frege, George Boole, Ramon Llull, and Kurt Gödel. Early computing advancements involved innovators such as Ismail al-Jazari, Kenneth E. Iverson, Per Brinch Hansen (concurrent computing/RPC), Lynn Conway (VLSI), and Edsger W. Dijkstra (structured programming), complemented by contributions from Geoffrey Hinton (backpropagation) and Jacek Karpiński (Perceptron/KAR-65).
Federico Faggin is significant in microelectronics, pioneering MOS silicon-gate technology (SGT). His contributions at Intel include co-developing the 4004 and 8080 microprocessors, designing the Fairchild 3708, and co-founding Zilog and Synaptics. Faggin has also explored quantum consciousness theories and received the National Medal of Technology and Innovation.
Grace Hopper was a pivotal computer scientist famous for coining the term "debugging" after finding a moth in a 1947 computer relay. After her work with the UNIVAC I, she strongly supported programming languages using English words, leading to compilers and influencing COBOL, while also promoting networked computing and setting testing standards. Beyond her technical impact, Hopper was a celebrated speaker, received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016, and passed away in 1992 at age 85. Her enduring legacy is honored through various recognitions, including a scholarship at Microsoft, recognition in the FIRST Robotics Competition, a professorship at Yale University, the naming of a major Google undersea network cable in 2020, and her role in establishing the yearly Grace Hopper Celebration of Women in Computing.
